etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English bely, beli, bali, below, belew, balyw, from Old English bielġ (“bag, pouch, bulge”), from Proto-West Germanic *balgi, *balgu, from Proto-Germanic *balgiz, *balguz (“skin, hide, bellows, bag”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰelǵʰ- (“to swell, blow up”). Cognate with Dutch balg, German Balg, Danish bælg, Old Irish bolg, Welsh bol. Doublet of bellows, blague, bulge, and budge. See also bellows.

definitions.definition: The abdomen, especially a fat one.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Jeremiah 1:5:
quote.text: Before I formed thee in the bellie, I knew thee;  […]

definitions.definition: The lower fuselage of an airplane.

quote.citation: 1994, Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom: The Autobiography of Nelson Mandela, London: Abacus, published 2010, page 454:
quote.text: There was no heat, and we shivered in the belly of the plane.

definitions.definition: The main curved portion of a knife blade.
(architecture) The hollow part of a curved or bent timber, the convex part of which is the back.
The part of anything which resembles (either closely or abstractly) the human belly in protuberance or in concavity; often, the fundus (innermost part).

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Jonah 2:2:
quote.text: […]  I cried by reason of mine affliction vnto the Lord, and hee heard mee; out of the belly of hell cried I, and thou heardest my voyce.

quote.citation: 1881–1882, Robert Louis Stevenson, Treasure Island, London; Paris: Cassell & Company, published 14 November 1883, →OCLC:
quote.text: At last I got my knife and cut the halyards. The peak dropped instantly, a great belly of loose canvas floated broad upon the water  […]

definitions.definition: To position one’s belly; to move on one’s belly.

quote.citation: 1903 July, Jack London, “The Sounding of the Call”, in The Call of the Wild, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., →OCLC, page 220:
quote.text: Bellying forward to the edge of the clearing, he found Hans, lying on his face, feathered with arrows like a porcupine.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To swell and become protuberant; to bulge or billow.

quote.citation: 1700, [John] Dryden, “Homer’s Ilias”, in Fables Ancient and Modern; […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC, book I, page 213:
quote.text: The Pow'r appeaſ'd, with Winds ſuffic'd the Sail, / The bellying Canvaſs ſtrutted with the Gale;  […]

quote.citation: 1890, Rudyard Kipling, The Rhyme of the Three Captains‎[1]:
quote.text: The halliards twanged against the tops, the bunting bellied broad,

quote.citation: 1914, Theodore Roosevelt, chapter 6, in Through the Brazilian Wilderness‎[2]:
quote.text: There were trees whose trunks bellied into huge swellings.

winds from sternward
Bore us onward with bellying canvas ...

quote.citation: 1930, Otis Adelbert Kline, The Prince of Peril, serialized in Argosy, Chapter 1,[3]
quote.text: The building stood on a circular foundation, and its walls, instead of mounting skyward in a straight line, bellied outward and then curved in again at the top.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To cause to swell out; to fill.

quote.citation: c. 1602, William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Troylus and Cressida”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene ii]:
quote.text: Your breath of full consent bellied his sails;  […]

quote.citation: 1920, Sinclair Lewis, chapter I, in Main Street: The Story of Carol Kennicott, New York, N.Y.: Harcourt, Brace and Howe, →OCLC:
quote.text: A breeze which had crossed a thousand miles of wheat-lands bellied her taffeta skirt in a line so graceful, so full of animation and moving beauty, that the heart of a chance watcher on the lower road tightened to wistfulness over her quality of suspended freedom.
